correctness.rationale: The definitions and depth criterion are those of Đurđev–Mudrinski. Let C_0=G and C_{i+1}=G C_i ∪ C_i G. This descending sequence is exactly the set of values at depth i: a depth-(i+1) term has a child at depth i, and any value on the other side is available as a depth-zero parameter. Thus 3-nilpotence gives C_3={0}. Failure of 3-supernilpotence gives a nonzero product in (G²)²⊆C_2 by Proposition 5.3. If two consecutive stages before C_2 were equal the recursion would stabilize, so G⊋C_1⊋C_2⊋{0}; at least four elements are needed. In the displayed table the three successive sets are {0,a,b}, {0,a}, {0}, with b²=a≠0. An independent bounded check iterated all tables with absorbing 0 (base-m digits for the (m−1)² nonzero-input cells), applied the recurrence three times, and tested C_1·C_1: orders 1,2,3 give respectively 1,2,81 tables, of which 1,1,3 are 3-nilpotent and none separates. The frozen check_minimal.py was inspected, not executed; the proof does not rely on it. This is only the two commutator notions at level 3 with absorbing zero, not a classification of all optimal tables.
